title: Cross-entropy and KL divergence (the loss behind LLMs)
summary: Cross-entropy H(p, q) = Σ p(x)·log(1/q(x)) is the average surprise when outcomes come from the truth p but are scored with the model q. It is never below the entropy H(p), and the gap is the KL divergence, which is zero only when q = p. For next-token prediction p is one-hot, so the loss at each position is simply −log q(correct token).
llm_link: This is the pre-training loss of GPT-style language models: the average over every position of −log q(actual next token). Minimising it is the same as minimising KL divergence to the data and the same as maximum likelihood. e raised to the average loss is the perplexity.
key_ideas: H(p, q) = Σ p(x)·log(1/q(x)) = −Σ p(x)·log q(x): outcomes drawn from p, surprise measured with q.
H(p, q) ≥ H(p), with equality only when q = p.
D_KL(p ‖ q) = Σ p(x)·log(p(x)/q(x)) = H(p, q) − H(p) ≥ 0, and in general D_KL(p ‖ q) ≠ D_KL(q ‖ p).
For a one-hot p on the correct token, H(p) = 0 and H(p, q) = −log q(correct token).
LLM loss = average of −log q(xₜ | x<ₜ) over all positions (natural log, nats); a uniform guess over V tokens scores ln V; perplexity = e^loss.

quiz.q: Predict the result: the model gives the correct next token probability 0.25. What is the cross-entropy loss at that position (natural log)?
quiz.explain: With a one-hot target the loss is −ln q(correct) = −ln 0.25 = ln 4 ≈ 1.386.

quiz.q: When is H(p, q) equal to H(p)?
quiz.explain: Cross-entropy is H(p) plus the KL divergence, and KL is zero only when the two distributions agree.

quiz.q: Why is KL divergence called a divergence rather than a distance?
options: It is not symmetric: D_KL(p ‖ q) usually differs from D_KL(q ‖ p)
quiz.explain: A distance must be symmetric. KL penalises q for missing what p considers likely very differently from q expecting things that p never produces.

quiz.q: An untrained model spreads probability evenly over a vocabulary of 50,000 tokens. Roughly what loss does it start at?
quiz.explain: Every correct token gets q = 1/50000, so the loss is ln 50000 ≈ 10.8 nats. Training brings it down from there.

quiz.q: A language model's average loss on some text is ln 20 ≈ 3.0 nats. What is its perplexity, and what does it mean?
options: 20: as uncertain as a fair choice among 20 tokens
quiz.explain: Perplexity = e^loss = e^(ln 20) = 20. On average the model is as unsure as if it were choosing uniformly among 20 tokens.

problems.title: Cross-entropy of two distributions
problems.prompt:
Write cross_entropy(p, q) = −Σ p(x)·ln q(x) for two lists of the same length, using math.log (natural log, so the answer is in nats).

Skip terms where p[i] == 0: they never happen, so they contribute nothing (and q may be 0 there).

cross_entropy([1, 0, 0], [0.5, 0.3, 0.2])            # 0.6931... = -ln 0.5
cross_entropy([0.5, 0.5], [0.5, 0.5])                # 0.6931... = H(p)
cross_entropy([0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.1], [0.62, 0.3, 0.06, 0.02])   # about 1.46
problems.starter:
import math

def cross_entropy(p, q):
    total = 0
    for pi, qi in zip(p, q):
        # TODO: skip pi == 0; otherwise subtract pi * log(qi)
        pass
    return total

tests.name: one-hot target
tests.code:
import math
out = cross_entropy([1, 0, 0], [0.5, 0.3, 0.2])
assert abs(out - math.log(2)) < 1e-12, f'with a one-hot p the loss is -ln q(correct) = -ln 0.5 = 0.693, got {out}'

tests.name: q equal to p gives the entropy
tests.code:
import math
out = cross_entropy([0.5, 0.5], [0.5, 0.5])
assert abs(out - math.log(2)) < 1e-12, f'when q = p, cross-entropy equals the entropy ln 2, got {out}'

tests.name: weather example
tests.code:
import math
p = [0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.1]; q = [0.62, 0.3, 0.06, 0.02]
exp = -sum(a * math.log(b) for a, b in zip(p, q))
out = cross_entropy(p, q)
assert abs(out - exp) < 1e-12, f'expected {exp:.4f}, got {out}. Each term is p * ln(1/q): weight by p, measure with q'

tests.name: zeros in p are skipped
tests.code:
out = cross_entropy([1, 0], [1.0, 0.0])
assert abs(out) < 1e-12, f'q gave probability 1 to the outcome that happened, so the loss is 0; got {out}. Skip p == 0 terms so log(0) is never called'

tests.name: positive
tests.code:
out = cross_entropy([0.2, 0.8], [0.6, 0.4])
assert out > 0, f'cross-entropy is a sum of positive surprises, got {out}. Did you forget the minus sign?'

hints: One line: -sum(pi * math.log(qi) for pi, qi in zip(p, q) if pi > 0)

problems.title: KL divergence and its asymmetry
problems.prompt:
Write kl(p, q) = Σ p(x)·ln(p(x)/q(x)), skipping terms with p[i] == 0.

Then check the two facts from the video: kl(p, q) == cross_entropy(p, q) − entropy(p), and kl(p, q) != kl(q, p) in general. (cross_entropy and entropy are provided.)

kl([0.5, 0.5], [0.5, 0.5])     # 0.0
kl([0.5, 0.5], [0.9, 0.1])     # 0.5108...
kl([0.9, 0.1], [0.5, 0.5])     # 0.3681...

tests.name: zero when equal
tests.code:
out = kl([0.2, 0.3, 0.5], [0.2, 0.3, 0.5])
assert out is not None, 'returned None'
assert abs(out) < 1e-12, f'KL of a distribution with itself is 0, got {out}'

tests.name: matches the definition
tests.code:
import math
out = kl([0.5, 0.5], [0.9, 0.1])
exp = 0.5 * math.log(0.5 / 0.9) + 0.5 * math.log(0.5 / 0.1)
assert abs(out - exp) < 1e-12, f'expected {exp:.4f}, got {out}. The ratio inside the log is p / q'

tests.name: cross-entropy = entropy + KL
tests.code:
p = [0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.1]; q = [0.62, 0.3, 0.06, 0.02]
assert abs(kl(p, q) - (cross_entropy(p, q) - entropy(p))) < 1e-12, 'KL should equal the gap between cross-entropy and entropy'

tests.name: not symmetric
tests.code:
a, b = kl([0.5, 0.5], [0.9, 0.1]), kl([0.9, 0.1], [0.5, 0.5])
assert abs(a - b) > 0.1, f'KL is not symmetric: expected different values, got {a:.4f} and {b:.4f}'

tests.name: never negative

hints: sum(pi * math.log(pi / qi) for pi, qi in zip(p, q) if pi > 0)

problems.title: The language-model loss (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
A model reads a sequence of T positions and at each one outputs a distribution over a vocabulary of V tokens: probs has shape (T, V), and each row sums to 1. targets has shape (T,) and holds the index of the token that actually came next at each position.

Write lm_loss(probs, targets) returning the tuple (loss, perplexity): the loss is the mean over positions of −ln(probability of the correct token), and the perplexity is eloss.

To pick one entry per row, use fancy indexing: probs[np.arange(T), targets] has shape (T,), row t, column targets[t].

probs = np.array([[0.5, 0.3, 0.2],
                  [0.1, 0.8, 0.1]])
lm_loss(probs, np.array([0, 1]))   # (0.458..., 1.581...)

tests.name: small example
tests.code:
import numpy as np
probs = np.array([[0.5, 0.3, 0.2], [0.1, 0.8, 0.1]])
out = lm_loss(probs, np.array([0, 1]))
assert out is not None, 'returned None'
loss, ppl = out
exp = (-np.log(0.5) - np.log(0.8)) / 2
assert abs(loss - exp) < 1e-12, f'expected mean(-ln 0.5, -ln 0.8) = {exp:.4f}, got {loss}. Pick column targets[t] from row t'

tests.name: perplexity
tests.code:
import numpy as np
probs = np.full((4, 20), 1 / 20)
loss, ppl = lm_loss(probs, np.array([3, 7, 0, 19]))
assert abs(ppl - 20) < 1e-9, f'a uniform guess over 20 tokens has perplexity 20, got {ppl}'

tests.name: untrained model
tests.code:
import numpy as np
V = 50000
probs = np.full((3, V), 1 / V)
loss, _ = lm_loss(probs, np.array([1, 2, 3]))
assert abs(loss - np.log(V)) < 1e-6, f'uniform over 50000 tokens should give ln(50000) = 10.82, got {loss}'

tests.name: uses the targets, not the max
tests.code:
import numpy as np
probs = np.array([[0.9, 0.1], [0.9, 0.1]])
loss, _ = lm_loss(probs, np.array([1, 1]))
assert abs(loss - (-np.log(0.1))) < 1e-12, f'the correct token had probability 0.1 at both positions, so the loss is -ln 0.1 = 2.303; got {loss}. Did you use the largest probability instead of the target column?'
